subtopic: REMISSION OF CERTAIN PERIODS OF SENTENCES IMPOSED ON PRISONERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall answer the question in the affirmative, but I must say the procedure will not amount to an amnesty. We will follow the procedure laid down at the time of the diamond jubilee of Her late Majesty Queen Victoria, and again at the diamond jubilee of confederation in 1927. speechtext:
I have not the tons milled but if my recollection serves me correctly I may say for the information of the house that the tons milled as of about ,a month ago were 25,000 daily approximately. The figures are readily available and if it is thought desirable to have them spread on the record I can get them later.
Hon. members will therefore see the importance of devoting all the moneys which the dominion can devote towards stimulating the search for minerals in the various provinces of Canada and the Northwest Territories. This expansion of gold milling, of course, concerns only one branch of the industry. Base metals at the moment do not
offer a great attraction because there probably is a world over-production. The copper above ground has been variously estimated at from 425,000 to 600,000 tons. In Canada we are fortunate with respect to the mining of base metals, particularly copper, because I am told by one of the biggest operators who is very close to the industry that about seventy-five per cent of Canada's copper is produced at less than five cents a pound. That is a wonderful record, disclosing great efficiency.
In respect to this vote, in the last thirty years our universities in Canada have built up departments devoted to the study of chemistry associated with mining, and largely by reason of the stimulation that was given to the mineral industry by the discoveries at Cobalt our universities yearly graduate a very large number of young men who have

Public Works Program
chosen the business of mining as their life work. Heretofore the geological survey has in the summer time taken on their geological parties many of these young men who have passed their second year, and then on up to graduates. This has been a very wonderful experience for these young men who are headed for mining engineering or geological work. Of course, at the present time these, young men are feeling and have felt the depressed times and are meeting with a good deal of difficulty.
My idea with respect to the expansion of geological work-I do not know whether I shall be believed or not, but I think generally I shall be-is not political in any sense. I only regret that this course could not have been adopted years ago and that a little more generosity might have been shown in assisting in the search for minerals in this country. I took occasion last evening to go over the observations made by hon. members of the house in the past five years when the estimates for Mines were up and that from all sides of the house an expression of regret and some criticism that the department was not provided with more moneys to be devoted to these and kindred industries. It is the intention of the government through myself to get in touch immediately with the various universities of Canada which have science courses devoted to geological work and to mining. This may be disappointing to members on both sides of the house but I would gladly receive from any member in this chamber suggestions as to young men falling within the class to which I have referred in order that they may have an opportunity to assist in carrying out this work. I trust that hon. members will not harbour the idea that this is being put forward by reason of an impending election or for political purposes.
It is proposed, and I have gone forward in anticipation that this measure will pass parliament, to organize 180 geological investigating parties. The approximate cost of each party will run around $4,000. Then as a result of their work there will be some expense over and above that in connection with the compilation of the information. While the work of these geological parties will take in the whole range of economically valuable minerals, yet it is my desire to direct their activities more to those places in Canada where the geological occurrence is favourable to the deposition of gold. We in our country are particularly and peculiarly favoured with respect to the chances of finding gold in commercial quantities and of a richness that it can foe worked at a profit. We have across

the northern part of Canada from coast to coast geological conditions that will challenge the courage, the enthusiasm and the capacity for effort of the Canadian people for thousands of years. Perhaps it is a very good thing that the Infinite Being in laying down the earth's surface hid away there riches so that they would not all be found at once. Canada is particularly favoured in this regard. A study of the type of men engaged in this industry will show the courage which it takes and the persistence which must be exhibited in the search for minerals. There are certain people who cannot get interested in the gold mining industry until the gold brick is being poured, when they become keenly interested. They are totally unacquainted and apparently do not want to become acquainted with the hazards and discouragements antecedent to the pouring of the brick. This industry offers an outlet for many of the young men of Canada and I believe the organization of these geological parties will start a work which will be of benefit to the prospectors and bring about an even greater increase in gold mills than the fine records I have just spread upon Hansard.

speechtext:
I am just as anxious as the hon. minister that the search for minerals should be carried on and as the minister himself has intimated we who are interested in mining on many occasions have stated that the w-ork should be furthered to the best advantage. I am not particularly interested in the discussion at the moment of present position of the mining industry as I believe the people generally have a fair idea of the conditions. If I were to discuss this matter I would probably say many things with which the minister would not agree; I might refer to the conditions brought about by the action of the present government. What we are interested in at the moment is where these parties are to work and when they are to do their work. I would point out that in the particulars of civil government estimates of the minister the only decreases shown are for a geologist and an assistant geologist. If it were decided at the time the estimates were prepared that we had too many geologists, when was it decided that we should spend a million dollars to put out 180 additional parties? I sympathize with the young men who find it impossible to get employment after leaving college, but I would point out to the minister that during the last year he has lost three of his best geologists. If there is so much unemployment why is it that these men have left the department? It is because they have found the private field much more remunerative. I do

not want to detain the committee but I should like the minister to tell us something definite as to where this work is to be carried on and whether it will be carried on in cooperation with the different provinces. Parties will be sent to every province, as well as the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, wherever conditions appear favourable for the possible deposition of gold ore. No parties will be sent to Prince Edward Island as it is known that that province has nothing along that line. The exact number of parties which will go into each province has not yet been determined but I can give the committee an approximate distribution of the parties. There will be approximately twelve parties in Nova Scotia; four in New Brunswick; fifteen in Quebec and thirty in Ontario. These figures are only approximate and I am inclined to the view that more parties will be sent into Quebec. There will be approximately twenty in northern Manitoba; forty in Saskatchewan, eight in Alberta; twenty in British Columbia; ten in the Northwest Territories and five in the Yukon. This is something which I have had in mind for many years, even before I became a member of this house. I .have always urged the
different governments to promote more activity in the mineral industries but I always realized the difficulty in providing money to carry out this work. The localities in which these parties will work have not been definitely determined but anyone who has studied the geological maps of Canada will know the districts favourable to the finding of gold bearing ore. These matters will be worked out by the officers of the department. It will not be possible to complete this work this year as the field notes will have to be transcribed and published after the parties return in the fall. The work will no doubt run into next year.

speechtext:
I certainly congratulate the government on bringing down this appropriation for geological surveys. As a practical mining man who goes into the field and prospects, I think I know something about the need for this sort of work. It has been said that 180 parties constitute a very

large number. I do not think it should be necessary for me to remind the committee that there is room for 180 geological parties in my constituency, to say nothing of the great areas in northern Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories which contain the same geological set up as does northern Manitoba. I am not going to discuss all classes of mining; I shall confine myself for the moment to gold mining. It is not necessary for me to remind the committee that gold mining has been the sheet anchor to which this country has tied itself during four of the darkest years Canada has ever experienced. Gold is a commodity that requires no sales staff and no sales talk; it has enabled this country to meet its obligations, thereby allowing us to maintain our national integrity.	.
Yesterday I heard the leader of the opposition enlarging upon the appropriation of $100,000 in the main estimates. I do not think anybody would be unfair enough to say that that is a proper allotment for this important industry that produces hundreds of millions of dollars worth of new wealth in this country at little or no cost to this government or to the taxpayers. Personally I am glad to see that all of the money in this vote is not going into piles of brick and stone in cities. Whether we like it or not, we have to look north. The future of this country lies in that great northern area, with its two million square miles of the pre-Cambrian, which is beckoning with a finger of gold, its message-"Come and get it"-and it is up to the government to lead the way. So far the lone prospector has had to carry most of the load; he has been left to do all the pioneering work. It is time that the government stepped in and gave him some assistance by way of opening up these fields, putting out these parties to make geological reports on the areas and issuing proper maps so that he may be better able to travel and know where he is going to work. Otherwise he will waste a great deal of time, for the season for prospecting in those northern areas is very short; he cannot get into the field until the end of June owing to ice conditions, and if he is very far north, he will have to hike out of there about September 15 or he will be liable to be frozen in. The minister has in his department I think the finest organization of its kind in the world, but due to lack of money so far they have been working under difficulties. This appopria-tion will give them an opportunity to do their stuff, and I am quite sure the government will receive large dividends from the investment.

Public Works Program
The once prevalent notion that the whole of the immense area north of the North Saskatchewan river was a sterile frost-bound waste destined for all time to remain a wilderness, is now largely a thing of the past, and the opportunities which the latent resources of the silent places of the unexploited north afford to the enterprising and adventurous, at the present moment challenges the attention of the whole world. The claim that Ontario would not be the province it is to-day had it not been for its progressive and courageous northern development policy, cannot be questioned. The same policy should be applied to those great northern areas. In conclusion I congratulate the government on at least awakening to its responsibility in regard to the mining industry of this country.

I am informed the section to which I refer is section 10, and turning to the bill I find it reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything contained in section 262 of the Railway Act, as enacted by chapter 43 of the statutes of 1928, and amended by chapter 54 of the statutes of 1929, the governor in council may in the case of any highway crossing of a railway determine the percentage of the cost which shall be payable out of the sum appropriated by this act to aid actual construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public.
The reason for the clause is that it has been found that at the present time, due to the difficult financial straits in which both the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways find themselves, they oppose any proposal to wipe out grade crossings, towards the work upon which they have to contribute. That practice has been followed in the past. The board of railway commissioners may receive an application either

from the railway or from a municipality- usually it is one of these two-asking for the elimination of a crossing. They look into the case, and from the grade crossing fund they may allot up to 40 per cent, but not higher than $100,000 to any crossing; that is, they may allot up to 40 per cent of the cost of the crossing. That is taken from the fund contributed by the government, and the balance is paid either by one railway or, in some cases by both of them, and by the municipalities concerned. At the present time neither the railways nor the municipalities want any allotment placed on them. As the committee is well aware municipalities are in financial difficulties and as a consequence do not wish to make contributions. That is why I said a moment ago to the hon. member that I do not think many grade crossings were eliminated last year and that is the reason.
At the same time we wish to have the grade crossings eliminated. Generally speaking the fund will be under the control of the board of railway commissioners, and so far as we are concerned we would be only too happy if it were all under their control, because in that event we would not in any way be entering into a controversy between the municipalities and the railways. However, in certain cases, such as the one to which the hon. member has referred, due to the railways or the municipalities or both refusing to contribute, it may be thought wise because of a particular danger at a certain railway crossing for the government to give permission under clause 10 of the bill to the board of railway commissioners to grant the total cost out of the railway crossing fund. Perhaps it
would be wise for me to say a word at once concerning the statement made a few moments ago by the Minister of Railways and Canals to the effect that if we are to have this measure assented to by five o'clock we must make more rapid progress than we are now making. While we on this side are anxious to expedite matters as much as possible I hope the government will not attempt to crowd us into the position of having the bill passed at all costs on the score that the deputy to His Excellency the Governor General is waiting to give assent to the bills. I would suggest that the government decide at once that the assent to whatever bills there may be will be given at a quarter past six o'clock to-night. We shall know by six o'clock whether or not we have received the information to which we are entitled before this measure passes.
I wish to repeat to-day not only what I said last night but my observations on the address in reply to the speech from the throne delivered at the opening of the session, namely, that we expected the government to bring forward its program in regard to unemployment relief or for providing employment at the early stages of the session, and did not expect it to be left until the moment of adjournment. Hon members will recall I indicated upon the first occasion we were quite prepared to facilitate the program of social reform, improvements to the capitalistic system and the like, but that we insisted that these particular measures should not be used to prevent the immediate consideration of that which we regarded and still regard as the most important of all problems, namely, the question of the unemployed and the giving of employment and affording relief.
The whole session has been taken up thus far in a discussion of measures other than those relating primarily to the great problem of unemployment now existing. As hon. members are well aware the provisions of the unemployment insurance measure will not come into effect for another year or two. The legislation concerning the weekly day of rest will not at the moment affect the unemployed, nor will these other measures of so-called social reform which have taken up time and discussion. They will not affect the present unemployment situation. Hon. members on this side of the house have from the beginning of the session emphasized the importance of giving the matter of unemployment consideration before anything else, and we particularly emphasized the importance of giving the house an opportunity to discover from the government whether or not they have any policy at all, or anything which could be called a policy with respect to unemployment.
This is the first opportunity we have had to discuss what the government may have in view with regard to relieving the situation. The debate which took place on a motion to go into supply was one which surely made evident to hon. gentlemen opposite our desire to get information and to discover what the government's policy was. However we received no answer from the government upon that occasion; we were given no indication as to what their policy was, and I do submit that if the present legislation is part of the unemployment program this house should have been given it long ago.
How does it come about, for example, that we have had before us for some time the estimates respecting geological surveys, and that only now have we had presented a program of exploration and investigation with respect to the mining industry, a program which certainly could most properly have been considered under the estimates for the surveys branch of the Department of Mines. Nothing was said on this point. Did the ministry have a program of this kind in mind when they were preparing the main estimates? If they had, why did they not put in the main estimates, under the heading of geological surveys, some indication that a larger appropriation would be required? Why did they not state upon that occasion that the appropriation would serve the double purpose of furthering exploration and investigation in connection with gold and other minerals in northern Canada, and at the same time help to create employment for some of those who were unemployed?
Public Works Program

We object strenuously to the fact that under the guise of helping to provide employment and to provide unemployment relief the government is really putting through a policy with respect to an important phase of business, and is placing before us as a matter primarily of relief what ought to have appeared in the main estimates as part of the general business of the country. The same is true in connection with what is being asked for by the Department of Railways and Canals. It is certainly true with regard to the Interior. It is equally true with regard to Public Works. There are works here in the nature of public works that ought to appear in the estimates of the Department of Public Works as part of the expenditure for public works throughout the country to be voted in the regular way.
One of the most ludicrous features of this measure is the clause which is inserted to the effect that if anything occurs in the nature of an emergency the government must be free to go ahead and spend a lot of this money in a way quite different from that in which it would be obliged to spend it under the regular appropriations of this parliament. What possible emergency can there be at the present moment in the mind of the administration other than the emergency of a general election which is to come along very shortly? I mean to say that if the government is contemplating emergencies arising in connection with the expenditure of these public moneys, surely we ought to have heard about them at the beginning of the session, and when the main estimates were brought in provision ought to have been made there for them. In last year's bill for relief we had the same expression used in respect to emergency, and the same provision was made for emergency, and yet the money asked for and voted to meet these possible emergent situations has not yet in very large part been expended.
What have we this morning in the way of information from the minister with regard to this one item? One thing we have been told is that we are being asked to vote one million dollars while the Minister of Mines does not think that that one million dollars can be spent. I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance whether he as Minister of Finance approves of that method of voting public money, asking parliament for millions of dollars without he himself or any of his colleagues even knowing *or being able to tell parliament how the money is to be spent. As a relief bill, it is a make-believe.

Mr. Chairman, I resist the temptation which comes to me to reply to the remarks of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, although I must say that I do feel sorely tempted to traverse the ground, but if I attempted to do so I would be consuming time which ought to be devoted to satisfying that eagerness for information which hon. gentlemen opposite exhibited last night and again this morning, and with respect to which I do not find any fault. I will, however, make this one observation, that I do not for a moment subscribe to the suggestion of my right hon. friend that this is a political measure. If we had thought to make it a political measure we have an example and a pattern which we could have followed by merely picking up the legislation which was brought down by my right hon. friend and his government on the eve of the general election of 1930. As a matter of fact the modesty of this appropriation in the light of existing circumstances in the country is I think a complete answer to the suggestion that there is anything political contained in the bill. speechtext: Perhaps I may be permitted to take a few minutes regarding this matter, for the circumstances are unusual and an exception to the situation which generally arises under the existing laws. It relates to twenty-six level crossings on a twenty-five mile stretch of the trans-Canada highway. This situation can be corrected only by the good will and cooperation of the two great railway systems, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, because these crossings can be removed by either railway taking running rights over the other. The two railways run parallel, at some places only five feet distant one from the other. This matter has been taken up with the railways and with the board of railway commissioners, but they have deferred doing anything about this dangerous situation by reason of the cost, or possibly because of hesitancy on the part of either railway to cooperate by granting running rights to the other, perhaps owing to the cost. But as some of this appropriation can be used under unusual conditions to supplement whatever the railways would ordinarily be required to pay under the existing law, I should like to ask that the Minister of Railways be kind enough to inform the board of railway commissioners and the railways affected that they can now remedy the situation by accepting the plan which has been suggested, which will do away with twenty-three level crossings. That station provides accommodation for the villages of Beachburg and Westmeath, and also for hundreds of individuals in the townships of Westmeath and Ross. This petition is signed by 185 farmers and business men in that section. The station was destroyed by fire in 1931, and since that time the management of the Canadian National have made no move to provide station accommodation for these people. They have fitted up an old railway coach at that point, but the accommodation is entirely inadequate. Because of the economic situation these people have been hesitant about asking the management of the Canadian National to provide a new station, but I think the time has come when the Minister
Public Works Program

of Railways should direct the attention of the management to this situation. Last year about $80,000 worth of freight traffic originated in that locality, consisting of shipments of live stock, grain, hay and pulpwood.
This Station is on the main line of the National Transcontinental, and the only passenger service is provided by two night trains, one going west at 11 p.m. and the other going east at about 4 a.m. This accommodation is entirely inadequate. The Canadian National come to this house and ask the taxpayers of this country to meet enormous obligations; they are looking for traffic for the road, and here is a locality that has provided an immense amount of traffic but receives no service in return. When those people wish to travel they must drive to this point at night, and very often the station is not even heated. Sometimes the transcontinental trains are three and four hours late, and the people are expected to wait in an old railway coach. Because they have aocepted the situation and have not made a vocal protest against it, the management of the Canadian National have simply ignored the needs of that locality. I notice in the daily press that the government are being asked to guarantee bonds of the Canadian National totalling $48,400,000, and I think in view of that situation the people in these localities should receive adequate service and accommodation. Previously a gasoline oar operated on this line; to-day there is absolutely no competition with the Canadian Pacific during the day-time. Formerly there was one local car east and west, from Ottawa to Pembroke, daily, and that served the people along that line. No doubt the Canadian National obtained a good deal of passenger traffic through that service, but even that has been discontinued.
While I am on my feet I should like to mention another matter. In almost all the important harbours in this country we have harbour commissioners to look after the business of the haibour, and from time to time they have borrowed money from the federal government to provide the necessary works in the harbours over which they preside, and the federal government has always charged them a certain rate of interest for the use of that money. So far as I personally am concerned I have never objected to the loaning of the money to these harbour commissions provided I felt the works were necessary for the welfare not only of that particular harbour but of Canada as a whole, and I am just wondering why at this late date we are now changing this policy which we have pursued for many, many years of making the harbour commissions responsible for the spending of money that is advanced to them, and responsible also for collecting sufficient dues to pay the interest on the money so borrowed and sufficient finally to liquidate the liability to the federal treasury. I cannot conceive that the policy has been changed simply for the purpose of providing unemployment relief, because after all is said and done the government of this country could well approach these various harbour -commissions and consult with them as to the possibility of providing work through legitimate construction deemed advisable in these harbours which would be of value to the country, and the expenditure could then be made under the jurisdiction of the commissioners, who would be responsible for the repayment of interest and the repayment of

Earlier in my observations I stated I had never made any objection to public works being conducted anywhere, so long as they were for the benefit of Canada, whether they were in the east or in the west. Any remarks I have made in this chamber since becoming a member of parliament will bear out my statement. It does appear to me however that we are not acting properly When we proceed on the assumption that we are going to relieve unemployment to a greater extent by making grants to harbour commissioners than by giving loans, as has been done in the past. That in my judgment is no substantial reason for a change of policy. I am just as anxious as the minister or any other hon. member to bring about relief of unemployment. I must say however that the past policy not only of this but of previous governments in dealing with harbour commissions has been by way of loans, placing the matter on a business basis so that the commissions would be responsible for the spending of the money loaned and for the dues and charges made to recover sufficient not only to pay the running expenses of the harbour but also to provide for interest on sinking fund. I say that is the best business basis upon which our harbours could be run. I am not satisfied with the answer the minister has given, notwithstanding the fact that the same principle was followed last year.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT

I do not wish to repeat what other hon. members have said; I rise simply to emphasize some of the points which have been made with regard to this unemployment measure. I have been looking carefully through the schedule, and
[Mr. Duranleau.)
for the life of me I cannot understand why the government did not bring down the proposed expenditures in the estimates. More than half of the $17,000,000 should have been included in the estimates, in which event we would have had plenty of time to discuss them. I cannot understand why the government have followed this course, except they wish it to appear that these are extraordinary expenditures being made in the interests of the unemployed.
Dredging is not going to help unemployment very much. True, repairs to wharves will give a certain amount of work, but I know, the Minister of Public Works knows and every other minister knows that those works could have been included in the estimates, in which event we would have had plenty of time to discuss them in committee of supply. However we are asked to accept these proposed expenditures which, properly speaking, are additions to the estimates; we are asked to accept this gesture which would have the people believe these expenditures are being made for the relief of unemployment. Other than the items which could have been placed in the .estimates I must say I can find in this bill very little help for the unemployed. It is true that the proposals offered by the Minister of Railways and Canals will undoubtedly create employment- there is some doubt as to whether or not those amounts are required, but I am not discussing that phase of the matter. Surely the government must realize that after five years in which serious conditions of unemployment have existed there still remains a similar condition, and undoubtedly we will have unemployment for some time. The government had plenty of time to include these items in the estimates.

speechtext:
I have not mentioned an election; I am talking about unemployment, and I think the hon. member understands. When he sat on this side of the house he was not one of the kindliest critics of government proposals-and I have no fault to find with that. We propose to say exactly what we think about these expenditures; we will do it here as well as in the country. All these harbour improvements could have been voted in the estimates. Items 3, 4. 6, 7, 13 and 14, including operations of nearly every governmental department, could have been voted in the estimates. But my hon. friend wants to camouflage by saying that this is an extraordinary expenditure that we must undertake to take care of unemployment. Yet all the time they have been in office they knew that unemployment was prevalent. I am not complaining about these proposals as an election gesture; I am only thankful that the amounts have not been increased very materially for election purposes. if that is any comfort to my hon. friends, but I do protest that the policy of this government ever since they have been in office has been to seek to secure money from parliament by means other than the legitimate means provided for so doing. speechtext:
We voted $40,000,000 last year, gave the government practically a blank cheque, and on the minister's own admission there was spent of that $40,000,000, in one of the most serious years for unemployment that has prevailed in Canada, only $10,000,000. That was I presume in order that the government would have more money to spend this year. One can come to no other conclusion. I do object, Mr. Chairman, as I have objected upon every occasion, to this method of doing business. Items that properly belong to the estimates and that we could properly discuss under the estimates are being asked for under this blank cheque method. Take the statement of the Minister of Marine. He can spend that $3,500,000 any way he likes provided he does a few of the things he has intimated will be done. There is nothing definite about his proposals of expenditure and he can make any changes that he sees fit. That is not the way that public business should be done. I have been waiting for some time to say it and I want to say it now as emphatically as I can: it is not the way public business should be done, and it is not the way public business was intended to be done.
I have left out of this estimate the one million dollars for grade crossings, also the one million dollars for geological surveys, both of which should quite properly have been included in the estimates, but I have given the government 'Credit for those two items and have classed them as extraordinary expenditures for the purpose of providing em-
Public Works Program

ployment. But all the rest of the items are everyday ordinary expenditures of the government, as I see it and as anounced by the ministers themselves when making their statements to the house with respect to all these items. They may have some difficulty in allocating all this expenditure, but I for one do not want to be accused of delaying the government for one single minute from getting busy and providing the necessary employment which God knows is badly enough needed in this country, and will continue to be needed so long as this government remains in office.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I have been looking over Bill No. 113, that we passed last year voting some forty million dollars for public works and I notice that in schedule A there are no less than ten items of work to be done for the city of Montreal. I am not complaining of that but apparently only one-quarter of the money that was allocated last year has been spent up to the present time, and in spite of that we now have an estimate before us for a further $3,500,000 to be spent on Montreal. I entirely agree with those who have preceded me in criticizing the way in which we are being asked to vote this money. I do feel that the proper way was to put these items in the estimates as usual.
There is one item in particular that I wish to draw to the attention of the government, and that is the item of $500,000 for western conservation works. It does seem to me that that is an infinitesimal amount to spend on that huge project; it will not begin to meet the difficulties we are facing in the dried out areas of western Canada. I should like to ask whichever minister is responsible whether he intends to come back to the house for a larger appropriation than $500,000 for this great project.

This is part of those various estimates, those that we figure we could arrange for. Then the Prescott elevator and the Port Colborne elevator are taken into account as part of the canal
	.
system. After the Prescott elevator was built, the workshop connected with it sank eight or nine inches and has to be put right. There is an estimate of $170,000 for that. In a few words I shall attempt to describe to the committee the main events. In 1912 the Toronto Harbour Commissioners presented to the dominion government their plans for waterfront improvements. At that time the federal government was requested to undertake the following works:	The western breakwater
from the Humber river to the western channel; an eastern sea wall from the eastern channel to Woodbine avenue; a ship channel, turning basin and marginal way walls in the eastern harbour terminal area; bascule bridges at the eastern and western channel entrances to Toronto harbour.
The recommendation was approved by P.C. 1426 dated June 10, 1913. The works to be performed by the city of Toronto were covered by an agreement dated December 14, 1914, and validated by the provincial Iegis-ture on April 8, 1916. The work to be done by the city covered the improvement of about 800 acres of park lands, the construction of a boulevard drive from the Humber river to Woodbine Avenue via Toronto island; a bascule bridge at Cherry street and works of a minor nature.
The work undertaken by the commissioners consisted of the reclamation of industrial and commercial sites from Bathurst street easterly, including the eastern harbour terminals with an area of over 1,000 acres, and the dockage development and reclamation on the inner harbour waterfront between Bathurst and Cherry streets. The works completed to date by the federal government are as follows:	Breakwater; ship channel;
turning basin and marginal way walls. The works yet to be undertaken by the federal government as provided by P.C. 1426 are as follows:
(1) Construction of bascule bridges at the western and eastern channel entrances to Toronto harbour.

'(2) Construction of the eastern sea wall from tihe eastern channel to Woodbine avenue.
The haribour commissioners have completed the reclamation of over 80 per cent of the projected works and constructed the dock walls and slips from Bathurst street to Yonge street including the bulkhead wall from Yonge street easterly to Parliament street. They have also constructed a bridge over the ship channel and completed Fleet street as a orosstown artery from Bathurst street to Cherry street, and Keating and Commissioners streets from Cherry street easterly to Leslie street.
I shall not weary the committee with further details, other than to say that the expenditures by the parties to the agreement to date are as follows:	The Toronto harbour
commission has spent $28,600,000; the federal government $8,000,000; the city of Toronto, including their share of grade separation costs, $8,000,000. I do not wish to delay the committee, but I consider this work to be of very great importance. Out of an expenditure of over forty million dollars the dominion government has spent only $8,000,000 and the financial set-up therefore is favourable to the dominion government. At the present time it is necessary either to construct a bridge to connect the western part of the island with the mainland, or something else to take the place of the abandoned idea of the bascule bridge. The tunnel is very much cheaper than the bridge, and the city has undertaken to assume the cost of maintenance, including paving and ventilation, thereby reducing the cost to the federal government to approximately $1,000,000.

There is no doubt that the construction of this tunnel will be a great convenience for perhaps a comparatively small number of Toronto people who will use it, but it seems to me that in connection with all the items that are on this program we ought to observe two factors particularly: first, is the work necessary and useful having regard to the amount of money which is to be expended; secondly, and this is also important, will it give the maximum amount of work for the amount of money that is to be expended? I was reading at the moment an editorial from the Toronto Clobe which touches on this very question of the tunnel. It is headed, Both Tunnel and Ferry, and reads in part as follows:
In these days of obligatory economy in the expenditure of public funds, Toronto is providing for the rest of the country a flagrant example of how not to economize. With becoming modesty, Mayor Simpson claims he played a part in inducing the dominion government to vote $1,100,000 for the building of a tunnel between the city and the island; and but a few days ago he and council authorized the expenditure of $77,000 on a new island ferry boat. What I cannot understand at the moment is why the federal government should spend this amount to connect one part of the city of Toronto with an island which belongs to the city. That is not a federal matter at all and this government has no right to vote a million dollars to connect one part of the city of Toronto with another part, whether it be an open field or an island. This island is just a playground and it has no federal significance whatever. I should like the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Matthews) or the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) to tell me why this government should spend a million dollars for a purely civic purpose.

speechtext:
The acting Prime Minister (Sir George Perley) had to proceed to the Senate chamber. He has prepared a statement which he intended to make and he has asked me to read it in his stead. It is as follows:
A few days ago I referred to the King George V Cancer Fund and the appeal that is being made by Their Excellencies, the Governor General and Lady Bessborough for subscriptions to it.
In view of the great interest that has been taken throughout the dominion in the twenty-fifth anniversary of His Majesty's accession
The Royal Assent

to the throne and the desire of the citizens of this country to associate themselves with His Majesty in his deep concern for the well being of his subjects, particularly as this fund is, by the special desire of His Majesty himself, to be used to assist in the eradication of the dread disease of cancer in this country, the government has decided to recommend to parliament that the sum of $100,000 be voted as a special thank offering gift from the entire population of this country to the King George V Cancer Fund for Canada.
